mainTopic: כתמים: שמואל's ground ruling, stains on different body parts, stains on looms and robes
overview: This amud first finishes discussing שמואל's ruling about a woman who checked the ground, sat on it, and found blood. רב ירמיה says she is pure by Torah law but טמאה מדרבנן. רב אשי says she is fully pure, because שמואל follows רבי נחמיה: something that cannot become טמא, like the ground, cannot carry כתמים. The גמרא then explains the משנה's rule about stains on the heel and the big toe. We do not assume blood moved from one place to another. The toe counts because it can end up right under the source while she walks, and the hand counts because every part of it may touch the source directly. Next, the 'inner side' of the leg is defined as reaching up to and including the knee joint (מקום חבק). רבי ירמיה asks about stains of unusual shapes, and an attempted proof is pushed away. רבי ינאי tells a woman who found blood on her loom to weave again as a test. The גמרא explains that a repeated test may be used to be stringent but not to be lenient. Finally, ברייתות discuss a robe worn at night, two women of different heights wearing the same robe, and a checked robe lent to a friend.

steps.title: End of רב ירמיה's answer: she is impure by rabbinic law
steps.stepSummary: The last word of רב ירמיה's answer shows that שמואל only meant she is טהורה מדאורייתא, but she is still טמאה מדרבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: …by rabbinic law.
steps.whatsHappening: This one word finishes רב ירמיה's answer from just before this section. שמואל's 'טהורה' means pure by Torah law only, while the רבנן still treat her as טמאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sources that call her טמאה were contradicting שמואל. רב ירמיה fixes this by splitting the levels of law: by Torah law she is pure because she felt nothing, but the רבנן declared her impure. This way שמואל and those sources agree.

keyTerms.meaning: By rabbinic law, a rule the חכמים added
By Torah law (the other half of רב ירמיה's answer)

steps.confusionAlert: This word is the END of a sentence that began before this section. Do not read it as a new statement. It completes רב ירמיה's answer: 'pure by Torah law, impure by rabbinic law.'

phrases.english: by rabbinic law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב ירמיה's answer, which began before this section, to the challenges against שמואל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting levels of law: Torah law versus rabbinic law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed that שמואל called her fully pure, which goes against the sources that call her impure.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל meant pure only by Torah law. By rabbinic law she is impure, so there is no contradiction.

steps.title: רב אשי: שמואל follows רבי נחמיה about stains on things that cannot become impure
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer: שמואל holds like רבי נחמיה, who says that anything that cannot become טמא, like the ground, cannot carry כתמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: שמואל said his ruling following רבי נחמיה, as we learned in a משנה: רבי נחמיה says, anything that cannot become ritually impure cannot become impure through blood stains either.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a second way to explain שמואל. He says she is fully pure, even by rabbinic law, because the blood was found on the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב אשי, the rabbinic rule of כתמים applies only to things that can become טמא, like clothing. The ground can never become טמא, so a stain on it does not make her impure at all. The sources that call her impure are talking about stains found on things that can become טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: Blood stains found on a body or an item; their impurity is a rabbinic rule
Anything that cannot become impure, such as the ground

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives us two different readings of שמואל. For רב ירמיה she is still impure by rabbinic law. For רב אשי she is fully pure, because of where the stain was found.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is Shmuel who spoke according to Rabbi Neḥemya,
as we learned in a mishna: Rabbi Neḥemya says:
phrases.notes: This משנה comes later, on דף נ״ט עמוד ב׳.

phrases.english: Any item that is not susceptible to ritual impurity
is not susceptible to impurity from stains.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: שְׁמוּאֵל הוּא דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי נְחֶמְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the same challenges that רב ירמיה answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Linking שמואל to a known תנא's opinion (רבי נחמיה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed that שמואל calling her pure goes against the sources that call her impure.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל follows רבי נחמיה: stains on the ground do not cause impurity at all. The other sources are talking about stains on items that can become impure.

steps.title: Why did שמואל say 'ground' according to רב ירמיה?
steps.stepSummary: Mentioning the ground makes sense for רב אשי, but for רב ירמיה the same ruling should apply to a cloak, so why mention the ground?
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for רב אשי; that is why שמואל said 'ground.' But according to רב ירמיה, why specifically the ground? Even a cloak should have the same ruling!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests both answers against שמואל's exact words. It challenges רב ירמיה: if the ground plays no special role in his reading, why did שמואל mention it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב אשי, the ground is the whole point, because it cannot become טמא. For רב ירמיה, the reason is that she did not feel anything, which is true whatever she sat on. So the detail 'ground' seems to add nothing, and a cloak should have been just as good.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This works fine for…', the opening of a challenge against the other view
'Why specifically this?' A challenge to a detail that seems unneeded
Ground, floor; it can never become ritually impure
A cloak, a garment that can become impure

phrases.english: Granted, according to Rav Ashi,
that is why he says 'ground,'
phrases.notes: 'He' is שמואל. The ground fits רב אשי because it cannot become impure.

phrases.english: but according to Rav Yirmeya,
why specifically the ground?
Even a cloak as well!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי הַיְינוּ דְּקָאָמַר קַרְקַע אֶלָּא לְרַב יִרְמְיָה מַאי אִירְיָא קַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two answers and attacks רב ירמיה's answer from שמואל's wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ירמיה's explanation of שמואל (pure מדאורייתא, impure מדרבנן)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If שמואל's reason does not depend on the ground, mentioning the ground is unneeded; a cloak should give the same ruling.

steps.title: שמואל used a 'not only this, but even that' style
steps.stepSummary: שמואל meant: obviously a cloak is pure, since it is hard to check and the blood may have come from elsewhere. He teaches that even the ground, which is easy to check, is pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: He spoke in the style of 'it is not necessary.' It is not necessary to say a cloak is pure, since it cannot be checked well and we can say the blood came from somewhere else. But even the ground, which can be checked well, so we might say the blood came from her body, is pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב ירמיה. שמואל chose the harder case, the ground, to show the ruling applies even there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cloak has folds and cannot be checked well, so the blood could easily have come from outside. That makes it an easy case. The ground can be checked fully, so blood found there more likely came from her. If she is pure even in that case, she is certainly pure with a cloak.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not needed to say…', a style that teaches the harder case so the easier one is obvious
It came from outside, from some other source

steps.whatToRemember: Two readings of שמואל: רב ירמיה says she is pure by Torah law but impure מדרבנן, and the ground is the harder case ('לא מיבעיא'). רב אשי says she is fully pure, following רבי נחמיה, because the ground cannot become טמא.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the ground is the EASIER case for רב ירמיה. For him it is the HARDER case, because the ground is checked well, so blood there more likely came from her. That is exactly why שמואל chose it.

phrases.english: He is speaking in the style of 'it is not necessary.'
It is not necessary to say this about a cloak,
which cannot be examined well,
and we can say it came from elsewhere,
but even the ground, which can be examined well,
so we could say it came from her body,
is pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רב ירמיה by explaining why שמואל mentioned the ground.
steps.terutzResolutionType: 'לא מיבעיא' style: the harder case is stated so the easier case is obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Mentioning the ground seemed unneeded for רב ירמיה, since a cloak should be the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ground is the harder case because it can be checked well. If even the ground is pure, a cloak certainly is.

steps.title: The משנה's ruling on heel and big toe stains
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: a stain on her heel or on the tip of her big toe makes her טמאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if a stain is found on her heel or on the tip of her big toe, she is impure, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה so that it can discuss it. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heel and the big toe are not close to the place blood comes from, yet the משנה still rules she is טמאה. The גמרא wants to understand why each of these spots counts.

keyTerms.meaning: The tip of her big toe

phrases.english: On her heel or on the tip of her big toe
she is impure, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל עֲקֵבָהּ וְעַל רֹאשׁ גּוּדָלָהּ טְמֵאָה וְכוּ׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה after the discussion of שמואל's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stain on the heel or the tip of the big toe makes the woman טמאה.

steps.title: Why does the big toe count?
steps.stepSummary: The heel makes sense because it touches the source when she sits. But what is the reason for the big toe?
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, the heel makes her impure, because the heel often touches that area. But the tip of the big toe, what is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the heel ruling and asks for the reason behind the big toe ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a woman sits or kneels, her heel can press against the place where blood comes out, so blood there is easy to explain. The big toe does not normally touch that area, so the גמרא asks how blood could have reached it.

phrases.english: Granted, her heel,
it tends to touch that place,
phrases.notes: "That place" is the area where the blood comes out. The heel can press there when she sits or kneels.

phrases.english: but the tip of her big toe, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the משנה quoted in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How blood could reach the tip of the big toe, so that a stain there makes her טמאה.

steps.title: Rejecting the idea that the toe touched the heel
steps.stepSummary: One might say the big toe sometimes touches the other heel. But we do not assume impurity moves from one place to another.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say the toe sometimes touches her heel, do we really assume impurity moves from place to place?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a possible answer to its question and immediately pushes it away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggested answer is that blood landed on the heel and then rubbed off onto the big toe. That would mean assuming the blood traveled from one body part to another, and the גמרא says we do not make that assumption.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a suggested answer)
We assume impurity moved from one place to another

steps.confusionAlert: The question "do we assume impurity moves from place to place?" is not a real question. It is a way of saying "we do NOT assume that."

phrases.english: And if you would say
sometimes it touches her heel,
phrases.notes: The idea is that the big toe of one foot rubs against the heel of the other foot.

phrases.english: but do we assume impurity
moved from place to place?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an answer to the question in step 6 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggested explanation that the big toe picked up the blood from the heel.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It depends on assuming impurity traveled from one place to another, which we do not assume.

steps.title: Challenge from the neck and shoulder wound
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a wound on the neck lets her blame the blood on the wound, but a wound on the shoulder does not. We do not say she may have carried the blood there with her hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: if she had a wound on her neck, where she can blame the blood on it, she may blame it. If the wound was on her shoulder, where she cannot blame it, she may not. And we do not say: perhaps she took the blood in her hand and brought it there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove the rule from step 7, that we do not assume blood moved from one place to another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blood from a shoulder wound could only reach the place where the stain was found if she carried it there by hand. The ברייתא says she may NOT blame the shoulder wound, which shows we do not imagine blood being moved from place to place. The same thinking rules out the idea that the toe got blood from the heel.

keyTerms.meaning: To attribute / she attributes (the blood to another cause, like a wound)

phrases.english: But it was taught in a ברייתא:
If she had a wound on her neck,
where she can attribute it, she attributes it,
on her shoulder, where she cannot attribute it,
she does not attribute it.
And we do not say
"perhaps she took it with her hand
and brought it there"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs the objection in step 7 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that we do not assume impurity moved from one place to another.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about a wound on the neck versus a wound on the shoulder.

steps.title: The big toe can end up under the source while walking
steps.stepSummary: The big toe is different: when she walks, it can happen to be right under the source, so blood can drip straight onto it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the tip of the big toe is different, because while she walks, it can happen to be in that position.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer to the question from step 6, explaining why a stain on the big toe makes her טמאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rejected answer needed the blood to pass from the heel to the toe. The new answer says blood can drip straight onto the toe while she walks, because the toe can end up right under the source. No moving of blood is needed, so the rule from step 8 is not broken.
steps.whatToRemember: A stain on the big toe is טמאה because the toe itself can be directly under the source while she walks, not because blood moved there from the heel.

phrases.english: Rather, the tip of her big toe is different,
since while she walks
it can happen to be there.
phrases.notes: He means the toe can end up right under the source, so blood drips straight onto it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6 with a new reason, replacing the answer rejected in step 7. That rejection was backed by the ברייתא in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New explanation of the case: blood reaches the toe directly.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The toe gets blood only by touching the heel, which would mean assuming blood moved from place to place.
steps.terutzMaskana: While walking, the toe can be directly under the source, so blood can reach it without moving from another spot.

steps.title: Challenge from a stain on the finger joints
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule that we do not assume impurity moved. A ברייתא says a stain on the finger joints is טמאה because hands touch everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: And do we really not assume impurity moved from place to place? But it was taught: if it was found on the joints of her fingers, she is impure, because hands are busy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks the rule from steps 7 and 8, using a ברייתא that seems to assume blood was carried by the hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blood does not normally fall straight onto the back of the fingers. The ברייתא still rules her טמאה because hands are always busy. The גמרא suspects this means blood was carried there from somewhere else, such as from the other hand, as the next step spells out. That would be assuming impurity moved from place to place, against the neck and shoulder ברייתא.

phrases.english: And do we not assume impurity moved from place to place?
But it was taught in a ברייתא:
If it was found on the joints of her fingers, she is impure,
because hands are busy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule that was proven in step 8 and relied on in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that we do not assume impurity moved from one place to another.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules a finger-joint stain טמאה because the hands may have carried the blood there, which seems to be exactly assuming impurity moved from place to place.

steps.title: Does the hand ruling show that impurity moves?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא presses the challenge. The ברייתא's ruling seems to be based on the idea that she checked with one hand and then touched the other hand. That would mean we do assume blood travels from place to place.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason for that ruling? Isn't it because we say: she checked herself with one hand and then touched the other hand?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out why the ברייתא from the last step seems to contradict our rule. Its ruling looks like it assumes blood was carried from one hand to the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 7 and 8 the rule was that we do not assume impurity moved from one spot to another. If the ברייתא makes her טמאה because one hand passed blood to the other, then it does assume movement. That would knock out the rule the big-toe discussion depended on.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not because...? (a question that sets up a challenge)

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He's asking about the ברייתא's ruling from the last step, that a stain on her hand makes her טמאה.

phrases.english: Is it not because we say:
she examined with one hand,
and touched the other hand?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge opened in step 10 by stating the reasoning it attacks.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that we do not assume impurity moved from place to place (steps 7–8).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling on the hand seems to work only if blood moved from the checking hand to the other hand. That would mean we do assume movement.

steps.title: The hand is different
steps.stepSummary: No. The hand is a special case, because any part of it may have touched the source directly. So no movement from hand to hand needs to be assumed.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Her hand is different, because all of it is likely to touch that place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It says the ruling about the hand is not about blood traveling. The hand itself may have touched the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hands are always moving and touching things. So any part of the hand, even the back, may have touched the source directly. The blood came straight from the source, not from the other hand. The rule that we do not assume impurity moves stays in place.
steps.whatToRemember: We still do not assume blood moved from one spot to another. The hand is different only because every part of it may touch the source directly.

phrases.english: No, her hand is different,
for all of it is likely to touch.
phrases.notes: He means the whole hand may have touched the source directly, so the blood did not need to come from the other hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case (the hand is unique)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ruling on the hand proves we assume blood moved from one hand to the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The hand may have touched the source directly, so no movement is assumed and the rule stands.

steps.title: How far up does 'inner side' go?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about stains on the inner side of the leg or feet. It asks how far up the leg the 'inner side' reaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: on her leg or on her feet, on the inner side, she is טמאה. On the inner side up to where?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes a line from the משנה and asks how high up the leg the 'inner side' goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blood dripping from the source can reach the inner side of the leg, so a stain there makes her טמאה. The משנה did not say where that area ends, so the גמרא asks for the upper limit.

keyTerms.meaning: her leg (the lower leg, the shin)

phrases.english: On her leg or on her feet,
on the inner side, etc.
On the inner side — up to where?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of whether impurity moves and returns to explain another line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The upper limit of the 'inner side' of the leg.

steps.title: Up to the knee joint
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי answers: the inner side goes up to the מקום חבק, the joint at the knee.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי said: up to the place of the joint.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer. The inner side of the leg goes up to the מקום חבק, the joint at the knee.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets the upper limit of the area where a stain makes her טמאה. One question remains: does the joint itself count as inside? Step 15 asks this, and step 16 answers it.

keyTerms.meaning: the place of the joint, where the thigh meets the shin at the knee

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai said:
Up to the place of the joint.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The inner side goes up to the מקום חבק (the knee joint).

steps.title: Is the joint itself inside or outside?
steps.stepSummary: A question is raised: does the מקום חבק itself count as part of the inner side or the outer side?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: is the place of the joint itself like the inside or like the outside?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about the answer it just gave. 'Up to the joint' could include the joint or stop just before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'up to' (עד) is unclear. It might mean up to and including the joint, so a stain on the joint makes her טמאה. Or it might mean up to the joint but not including it, so she stays טהורה. The question is about where the line falls exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: a question was raised before them (an open question)

steps.confusionAlert: Remember that 'up to' does not tell us whether the endpoint itself is included. That is exactly what is being asked here.

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
Is the place of the joint like the inside or like the outside?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for more detail about the answer given in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the joint itself is included in the inner area.

steps.title: רב קטינא: the joint counts as inside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a teaching of רב קטינא: up to the joint, and the joint itself counts as the inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב קטינא teaches: up to the place of the joint, and the joint itself is like the inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a teaching from רב קטינא. The joint itself counts as the inner side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב קטינא's wording says outright that the joint is included. So a stain right on the joint makes her טמאה, and the question from step 15 is settled.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rav Ketina teaches:
up to the place of the joint,
and the joint itself is like the inside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15 from a teaching of רב קטינא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The joint itself counts as the inner side.

steps.title: Another version puts it in רבי ינאי's school's own words
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בריה דרב אויא teaches it outright as the words of רבי ינאי's school itself: up to the joint, and the joint itself is like the inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא son of רב אויא teaches it outright: the school of רבי ינאי said: up to the place of the joint, and the joint itself is like the inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another way the teaching was passed down. In this version, the line 'the joint itself is like the inside' is part of what רבי ינאי's school said in the first place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, only רב קטינא spelled out that the joint is included. Here, רבי ינאי's school says it themselves, so the question never even comes up. Both versions end with the same ruling.
steps.whatToRemember: A stain on the inner side of the leg, up to and including the knee joint (מקום חבק), makes her טמאה.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥiyya, son of Rav Avya,
teaches it outright:
the school of Rabbi Yannai said:
up to the place of the joint,
and the joint itself is like the inside.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִיָּיא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא מַתְנֵי לַהּ בְּהֶדְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up step 16 with another version of רבי ינאי's school's statement that already includes the answer.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling that the joint itself counts as inside.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב חייא בריה דרב אויא's version of the statement of רבי ינאי's school.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה asks about stains of different shapes
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks what the law is when the stain is shaped like a bracelet, a straight line, a row of drops, or runs across the width of her thigh.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: if the stain is like a bracelet, what is the law? If it is like a line, what is the law? If it is drops after drops, what is the law? If it goes across the width of her thigh, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה asks a set of new questions about stains with unusual shapes. This sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blood dripping down from the source usually lands in certain ways. A ring around the leg, a straight line, a row of drops, or a stain across the thigh might not look like dripping. That could suggest it came from somewhere else. רבי ירמיה wants to know if these shapes change the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: like a bracelet (a ring all around)
drop after drop (a row of drops)
across the width of her thigh

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
"Like a bracelet" — what is the law?
"Like a line" — what is the law?
"Drops after drops" — what is the law?
"Across the width of her thigh" — what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new set of questions about stains of unusual shapes on the body.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether stains shaped like a bracelet, a line, a row of drops, or running across the thigh make her טמאה.

steps.title: Trying to answer רבי ירמיה from a ברייתא about a stain on her flesh
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: a stain on her flesh that may be טמא or may be טהור is treated as טמא. It suggests this covers רבי ירמיה's oddly shaped stains.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If a stain is on her flesh and it is unclear whether it is impure or pure, it is impure. 'On her flesh'. Isn't this talking about a case like the ones רבי ירמיה asked about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer רבי ירמיה's question from Step 18 by quoting a ברייתא that says a doubtful stain on her flesh is טמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ירמיה asked about stains with unusual shapes, which might not look like they came from her body. The ברייתא speaks of a stain on her flesh that is a ספק and still rules it טמא. The גמרא suggests the 'doubt' here is exactly the unusual-shape case, which would mean those stains are also טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: A doubt; a case where we are not sure
'Isn't it that...?', the way the גמרא suggests a reading in order to prove something
In a case like this one

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If a stain is on her flesh,
and it may be impure or may be pure, it is impure.
'On her flesh':
isn't it talking about a case like this?
phrases.notes: 'A case like this' means the oddly shaped stains רבי ירמיה asked about in the last step.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to answer רבי ירמיה's question from Step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That stains shaped like a bracelet, a line, drops, or across the thigh are טמא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: a doubtful stain on her flesh is טמא.

steps.title: The ברייתא may only mean a strip-shaped stain
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: the ברייתא might be speaking only of a stain shaped like a strip, not the unusual shapes רבי ירמיה asked about.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Perhaps it is talking about a stain shaped like a strip.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof: the ברייתא could be talking about a normal, strip-shaped stain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A strip running down the length of the thigh is the usual shape of blood coming from her body, so it makes sense to call it טמא. That tells us nothing about bracelet-shaped, drop-shaped or sideways stains. So רבי ירמיה's question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps; maybe it is a different case
A strip, like a long band

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as ruling the unusual shapes טהור. The גמרא only says this ברייתא does not prove anything about them.

phrases.english: No, perhaps it is shaped like a strip.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in Step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from this ברייתא; the question of רבי ירמיה is left unresolved.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as dealing only with a standard strip-shaped stain.

steps.title: The woman who found blood on the loom threads
steps.stepSummary: A woman found blood on the warp threads of her loom. רבי ינאי told her to go and weave again to see whether the threads reach between her legs.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain woman found blood on the warp threads of her loom. She came before רבי ינאי. He said to her: Let her go and come, meaning go weave again and test it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a woman who found blood on her loom, and רבי ינאי's instruction to test it by weaving again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that while weaving, the threads touched between her legs and picked up blood from her body. רבי ינאי tells her to repeat her normal weaving to see if the threads really reach that spot. If they do, the blood might be from her; if they don't, there is no reason to connect it to her.

keyTerms.meaning: The warp: the long threads stretched on a loom
'Let her go and come': go repeat the action and see what happens

phrases.english: A certain woman
found blood on the warp threads of her loom,
she came before רבי ינאי,
he said to her: Let her go and come.
phrases.notes: He means: go weave the way you always do, and see whether the threads reach between your legs.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהִיא אִיתְּתָא דְּאִשְׁתְּכַח לַהּ דְּמָא בְּמַשְׁתִּיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about blood found on an object near her, not on her body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ינאי ruled that she should repeat her weaving to test whether the threads reach her body.

steps.title: But we do not rely on repeating an action in matters of טהרות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי ינאי's test with a ברייתא: in matters of purity, we do not rely on repeating an action to figure out what happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught: We do not test by repeating in matters of purity!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ינאי's instruction by quoting a ברייתא that forbids relying on a repeated action in purity matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A second try might not happen exactly like the first, so the test cannot prove what happened the first time. That seems to make רבי ינאי's 'go weave again' test useless here.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not repeat; we do not rely on redoing an action as a test

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: One does not repeat in matters of purity!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי ינאי's ruling in Step 21.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says repeated actions are not relied on in purity matters, so the test should not count.

steps.title: The rule only applies to leniency, not stringency
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: we don't rely on a repeated action to be lenient, but we do rely on it to be stringent.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we say we do not rely on repeating, that is to be lenient. But to be stringent, we do rely on repeating.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the rule of אין שונין to cases where the test would make things more lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right now the woman is טהורה, since the blood was not on her body or clothes. The test can only make her טמאה, never more lenient. Since it can only lead to a חומרא, the rule against relying on repetition does not apply.
steps.whatToRemember: אין שונין בטהרות: a repeated test can't be used to be lenient, but it can be used to be stringent. That is why רבי ינאי's weaving test is valid.

phrases.english: When we say one does not repeat, that is to be lenient,
but to be stringent, one does repeat.
phrases.notes: Here the test can only make her impure, since without it she would stay pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule (קולא versus חומרא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אין שונין forbids any reliance on a repeated action in purity matters.
steps.terutzMaskana: It only forbids relying on repetition to be lenient; relying on it to be stringent is allowed.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about a robe she takes off
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the next line of the משנה: a robe she takes off and covers herself with at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If she would take it off, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of a robe worn at night. It is setting up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that with such a robe, a stain anywhere on it makes her טמאה. The robe moves around while she sleeps, so any spot could have touched her body.

keyTerms.meaning: She takes it off (and uses it as a cover at night)
Etc.: the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: If she would take it off, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stain anywhere on a robe she covers herself with at night makes her טמאה.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר ברבי יוסי ruled stringently in Rome and was approved
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי אליעזר ברבי יוסי ruled stringently on this robe case in Rome, and the חכמים in the south told him he ruled well.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי אליעזר ברבי יוסי said: I ruled this matter stringently in the city of Rome, and when I came to the Sages in the south, they said to me: You ruled well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up the משנה's stringent ruling about the night robe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר ברבי יוסי ruled the woman טמאה in this robe case. The חכמים of the south approved, which confirms the משנה's stringent ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: I ruled; I gave a halachic decision
The Sages in the south of ארץ ישראל
You ruled well; you ruled correctly

steps.whatToRemember: For a robe she covers herself with at night, a stain anywhere on it makes her טמאה. This was ruled in practice and approved by the חכמים.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: It was taught: רבי אליעזר son of רבי יוסי said:
This matter I ruled
in the city of Rome, stringently,
and when I came to the Sages in the south,
they said to me: You ruled well.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the משנה line quoted in Step 24.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's stringent ruling about a robe worn at night.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: רבי אליעזר ברבי יוסי's ruling in Rome, approved by the חכמים of the south.

steps.title: A tall woman and a short woman swap robes
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules on a stain found on a robe that both a tall woman and a short woman wore. The height of the stain decides who is טמאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: a tall woman wore a short woman's robe, or a short woman wore a tall woman's robe. If the stain reaches the spot opposite the tall woman's private area, both women are טמאות. If not, the tall woman is טהורה and the short woman is טמאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a robe worn by two women of different heights, with a stain found on it afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same robe sits at different heights on different bodies. On the robe, the short woman's body lines up higher than the tall woman's. Blood flows down, so a stain at or below the tall woman's level could have come from either woman, and both are טמאות. A stain higher than that could not have come from the tall woman, so only the short woman is טמאה.

keyTerms.meaning: The private area of a woman's body, where blood would come from
Both of them are ritually impure

steps.confusionAlert: 'If not' means the stain is HIGHER than the tall woman's private area. Blood flows down, not up, so it cannot be hers. On the short woman, whose body lines up higher on the robe, the stain can still be from her.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A tall woman who wore the robe of a short woman,
and a short woman who wore the robe of a tall woman —

phrases.aramaic: אִם מַגִּיעַ כְּנֶגֶד בֵּית הַתּוּרְפָּה שֶׁל אֲרוּכָּה,
phrases.english: if it reaches opposite the private area of the tall woman,
both of them are impure.
And if not,
the tall one is pure and the short one is impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֲרוּכָּה שֶׁלָּבְשָׁה חֲלוּקָהּ שֶׁל קְצָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of stains on a robe and adds a new case with two women who wore the same robe.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the stain reaches the tall woman's private area, both are טמאות. Otherwise only the short woman is טמאה.

steps.title: A checked robe lent to a friend
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא: a woman checked her robe and lent it to her friend. The lender is טהורה, and the friend can attribute the stain to her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: a woman checked her robe and then lent it to her friend. The lender is טהורה, and her friend may attribute the stain to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא about a robe that was checked, lent out, and then found with a stain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender checked the robe and found it clean, so she is טהורה. Even so, the borrower is allowed to point to the lender and say the stain may be hers. This sets up רב ששת's question about what exactly that means.

keyTerms.meaning: She may attribute (the stain) to her

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
She checked her robe and lent it to her friend,
she is pure
and her friend may attribute it to her.
phrases.notes: The friend can say: maybe the stain is yours, because I don't rely on your check.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: בָּדְקָה חֲלוּקָהּ וְהִשְׁאִילַתּוּ לַחֲבֶירְתָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second ברייתא about two women and one robe. This time the robe was checked first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lender is טהורה, and the borrower may attribute the stain to the lender.

steps.title: רב ששת: the borrower's claim only helps in a money question
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the borrower's claim only helps in a money question. For טומאה, the lender is טהורה and the borrower is טמאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: this was taught about a money judgment. But regarding טומאה, the lender is טהורה and her friend is טמאה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת explains the ברייתא from the previous step and limits how far its ruling goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "her friend may attribute it to her" could sound like the borrower becomes טהורה. רב ששת says no. That claim only matters for a money dispute, such as who pays to wash the robe. For טומאה, the lender's check is trusted, so the stain falls on the borrower and she is טמאה.
steps.whatToRemember: In the tall/short case, the stain's height decides who is טמאה. In the lent-robe case, the lender who checked is טהורה and the borrower is טמאה. The borrower's claim (תולה) only helps her in a money dispute.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read "תולה בה" as making the borrower טהורה. According to רב ששת, she is still טמאה. She can only use the claim in a money question.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that one ruling can mean different things in different areas of הלכה. A claim that works in a money dispute does not decide questions of טהרה.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
We learned this regarding a monetary judgment,
phrases.notes: He means a money question, such as which woman has to pay for washing the robe.

phrases.english: but regarding impurity —
she is pure and her friend is impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: וּלְעִנְיַן דִּינָא תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the ruling of the previous ברייתא and limits it to money questions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The borrower's claim only applies to a money dispute. For טומאה, the lender is טהורה and the borrower is טמאה.
